description: The seminar examines Africans in dispersion/Diaspora as students interrogate the African background of African Americans and links between Africans and African Americans. The course examines the dynamics of precolonial West African societies; the nature of the interaction between Africa and the New World; and the role Africans, African culture, and African institutions played in the political, economic, cultural, and religious life of the New World. Students examine the ties that bind Africans and African Americans and explore questions such as: To what extent was the iconography of Africa used to mobilize Africans in dispersion? How effectively was the consciousness of Africa sustained in the New World? What are the contributions of African Americans to Africa? Also counts toward history, race and ethnic studies, and social studies education majors, and race and ethnic studies concentration.
name: Sem: Africa/Americas
title: Africa and the Americas: The Diaspora Experience

description: In this course, students explore the early medieval period, a time of dynamic transformation. Migrating and conquering cultures brought new approaches to art and architecture that forever changed the visual landscape of the early medieval world. Students examine the art of the Christian empires of the Mediterranean, the monastic traditions of Egypt and Nubia, Germanic cultures (the barbarians), the Islamic caliphate in Spain, and the Carolingians and Ottonians in northern Europe.

description: This course introduces students to global Indigenous artistic traditions, with case studies drawn from cultures including the Lakota (United States), Ainu (Japan), Sámi (Scandinavia), Inuit (Canada), Maori (Aotearoa/New Zealand), and Yanomami (Brazil), among others. Through close analysis of visual and material practices, the course examines how Indigenous artists represent their own communities and how those communities have been represented by others. Students will explore the relationships between art, cultural sovereignty, and knowledge transmission, with particular attention to both tangible and intangible heritage, including artistic practices, oral traditions, and foodways. The course considers the ongoing challenges posed by colonial histories and contemporary museum practices, as well as the strategies Indigenous communities employ to sustain and revitalize cultural traditions. Working closely with objects from the Flaten Art Museum's collection--including a recent acquisition of Inuit prints--students will engage in object-based learning and may participate in collaborative projects with the museum, with emphasis on critical looking, ethical interpretation, and the role of museums in shaping understandings of Indigenous art.

description: How do animals do what they need to do to survive in all sorts of environments? Why are others able to exist in only very particular conditions? These are the sorts of questions students explore as they navigate the basic systems that provide circulation, ventilation, movement, digestion, and waste removal. Students look at how these processes are coordinated by the nervous and endocrine systems and how they vary across the animal kingdom to help organisms survive in dry, hot deserts, in dark, deep oceans, and places in between. Students attend lectures plus one three-hour laboratory per week. In laboratory, they conduct quantitative physiological measurements to assess functions such as temperature control, respiration rates, and salt and water balance. Counts as "comparative organismal biology" core category. Offered periodically. Prerequisites: BIO 150; BIO 227 recommended.

Laboratories are designed to introduce students to the major invertebrate groups via observation of living animals and through dissection. Students attend lectures plus one three-hour laboratory per week. Counts as "comparative organismal biology" core category. Also counts toward neuroscience concentration. Prerequisites: BIO 150.

description: What makes a microscopic sequence of genetic code one of the most powerful forces on Earth? This course explores the fascinating world of viruses, from their elegant morphology to the complex machinery they use to hijack host cells. We will dissect the life cycles of major human pathogens, examining how they spread, evade the immune system, and cause disease. Beyond the biology of infection, we will discuss the development of vaccines, the rise of emerging global threats, and the cutting-edge use of viruses as tools for gene therapy. Prerequisite: BIO 150; recommended: BIO 227, BIO 231, or BIO 233.

description: This course surveys the geographic patterns of economic activity, with a focus on cities. It examines issues related to history, efficiency, and governance. The course introduces and applies several economic frameworks, including gains from specialization and trade, location theory, central place theory, migration, real estate valuation, rent analysis, income--expenditure models, consumer and producer choice, and public choice.These perspectives will be applied to several important questions: Why do cities develop and grow? What makes them so prosperous? How and why do cities differ? What economic problems commonly arise in them? How can local governments work to solve those problems? How might state and federal programs complicate matters? Will cities continue to promise growth and prosperity in the future? Adding the human dimension and real-world complexity to economic theory, we will also explore urban issues through an applied project. Groups of three to five students will select a city of their choice and investigate a specific urban issue, examining local problems, services, and ventures and report their findings. Romance, marriage, family, interracial relations, mothers and daughters, urban environments, gender politics and sexual violence, relations among females, intergenerational depictions, historical experiences, public expression and private reflections, individual and communal identities, class considerations--all of these and more images and themes arise in the fictional readings required for this course. description: This course examines the process of literary development in English during two consecutive and contrasting movements: the Neoclassical (1660-1780) and Romantic (1780-1840). Students read the works of representative and important writers from both periods, including Pope, Swift, Austen, Wordsworth, Blake, Shelley, Emerson, Douglass, and others, and examine the development of styles, conventions, and forms in English, Irish, and American literatures. Offered periodically. Prerequisite: WRIT 120 or equivalent.

description: Frederic Jameson has described conspiracy theory as a form of cognitive mapping that attempts "to think a system so vast that it cannot be encompassed by the natural and historically developed categories of perception." Engaging with both literature and film, this course invites students to think about how conspiracy narratives reflect and manage the anxieties and fears that accompany the totalizing conditions of late-stage capitalism, state surveillance and violence, media consolidation, and so on. Students study the form these narratives take, while paying special attention to allegory, detection, and conspiracy's "paranoid style." Topics include alien abduction, the assassination plot, government overreach, space exploration, mind control, medical treatment, and ecological disaster. Prerequisite: WRIT 120 or equivalent.

description: In this fiction writing course, students will read works of fabulism and horror and write stories of their own in these genres. "Fabulism" is a term often used interchangeably with "magical realism" to describe a mode of literature in which the fantastical and surreal are interwoven with the fabric of everyday life. This course will unpack fabulism's complexity and possibilities for a fiction writer. Students will write two original stories, workshop each, then choose one for revision at the end of the semester. Prerequisite: WRIT 120 or equivalent.

description: In this course, students read a series of memoirs to investigate the way Christianity has shaped individual people. From snake-handling to baptism, from icon-kissing to communion, from creeds to purity promises, Christian beliefs and practices can, by turns, prove to be life-giving, oppressive, disturbing, and salvific. How does emphasizing differing aspects of theology result in differing attitudes toward sexuality, gender, race, and the environment? In addition to approaching the memoirs from a critical perspective, students also identify and practice craft techniques as they write their own personal religious (or areligious) narratives. description: In this course, we’ll be exploring environmental storytelling and stories. What are the important elements of storytelling? And what exactly is an environmental story? Defining "environmental stories" is a little mysterious, hard to put in a box or wrestle into a paragraph because the word "environment" itself contains pretty much everything. Environmental stories can contain genres (such as science writing, nature writing, climate writing or journalism) but at their core, they must contain a story with stakes for the reader and the author and the environment itself. People tell stories to turn abstract patterns into opportunities for action. They tell stories to empathize, mobilize, find villains, celebrate heroes, give credit, assign blame, experiment with new ways of thinking, make sense of their experiences, and call for action. And listening to and telling stories are actions in their own rights.

description: This course will move beyond Hollywood and popular cinema's proposals of celebrity, assimilation, and visibility as the ultimate markers of liberation for trans and gender-nonconforming people. How have queer filmmakers used the audio, visual, and temporal components of cinema to transform reality into uniquely queer worlds? Students will engage directly with queer cinema, analyzing the formal techniques at play and their effect on the viewer. Film genres include musicals, melodrama, war films, comedy, westerns, horror and sci-fi films.

description: Throughout history, gardens have been spaces of cultivation, experimentation, discovery, and reflection. Many notable artists and thinkers have turned to gardening as both a refuge and exploration of being in right-relationship with the natural world. How can gardens help us to navigate the complexities of contemporary life as sites where we can explore alternative ways of collaborating with human and non-human beings? Can a hopeful, constructive imagination be cultivated through the practice of gardening? In this First-Year Seminar we will consider these questions by reading a variety of texts, holding small-group and full-class discussions, and writing regular reflective journal entries. We will also visit several local gardens and green spaces where we will practice slow looking and field drawing/journaling. Our semester will culminate in the creation of a collaborative, hand-bound book about (literal, imagined, or metaphorical) gardens with written and visual entries from each class participant.
name: Top: Creatives in the Garden
notes: Section topic: Creatives in the Garden

description: Dutch Historian Johan Huizinga designates the spaces in which we play games as "temporary worlds within the ordinary world, dedicated to the performance of an act apart." One might say the same of college, a particular kind of space where students come together to learn and grow in ways that prepare them to thrive in the "ordinary world" they enter after graduation. Students in this seminar will draw from the world of tabletop games and texts about games (both practical and philosophical) to learn how to apply good game design to creating a productive and enjoyable college experience. Students will discuss readings, play a variety of tabletop games (some educational and some designed for leisure), and work in groups to create, prototype, and playtest games every few weeks. Students will end the term with one revised and polished game. Writing will include design documents, instructional and marketing text, and reflections.

description: While ideas abound about how best to solve problems in the "Middle East," few understand the extreme diversity of the region or the political fault lines that undergird the various regimes currently holding power. While many Americans have recently developed an intense fascination with the "Question of Palestine," few understand how that issue fits into the broader set of questions that plague what has only recently been labeled the "Middle East." In this course, we will examine the emergence of the "Modern Middle East" out of the wreckage of the World Wars and the disintegration of empires that those wars wrought. We will learn to situate the conflict in Palestine within the broader trends of Arab nationalism and, later, rising Islamism. We will take the influence of religions and religious narratives on the region seriously without resorting to maximalist caricatures. Ultimately, we will weave together a broad contextual understanding in which to situate the conflicts we see daily reflected in our news outlets and social media feeds.

description: This seminar explores the development of the discipline of history, from its beginnings in the Ancient world to the present. Students investigate methodological and stylistic innovations in the Medieval and Early Modern periods that later formed the basis for history's emergence as an academic discipline in the nineteenth century. It features intellectual trends that have transformed historical research and writing over the last one-hundred years, resulting in a number of important "turns" influenced by other disciplines, ranging from sociology and anthropology to linguistics. In addition to reading some of the most influential texts in the discipline, students conduct research on a historiographical topic of their choosing.

description: How and why did the utopian dreams of nineteenth-century European intellectuals become the ideological justifications for twentieth-century totalitarian regimes? How did theBolshevik revolution in the name of the workers and oppressed peoples lead to authoritarianism and mass terror? How were nineteenth-century romantic dreams of a unified German Volk appropriated in service to a racialized "Volksgemeinschaft" that fueled Nazi violence? This seminar begins with the intellectual history of utopianism. Inverted social hierarchies and re-conceptualized means of correcting or preventing injustice are favorite tropes in utopian literature and in plans for creating utopian societies. To our modern ears, this sounds progressive, no? If only we could redesign society with justice and individual human freedom in mind, everyone would benefit, right? Our task will be to consider where and how this type of thinking produces opportunities for greater equity and equality while also laying the groundwork for future exclusivity. The heart of the course will consider the two greatest perversions of utopianism in European history and their deadly, tragic consequences: Stalinism and Nazism. Through primary sources and scholarship on the "history of everyday life," we will encounter a range of lived experiences of utopias in the making in the USSR and Germany.
name: Sem: Utopia and Terror

description: In the first half of the course, we will examine the "History" of the Holocaust, and establish a firm grounding in the historical context of the Third Reich and the genocide of the European Jewry. We will pay particular attention to Germany's development of a "Racial State" which defined who was and was not part of the Volk, and the legal, social, and economic steps the state took to exclude and persecute a range of the people they deemed "racially inferior"--Jews, but also the Roma and Scintii, people with developmental and physical disabilities, homosexuals, Slavs, and others. In the second half of the course, we will focus on ways the Holocaust has been remembered. After we've gained an overview of the Holocaust, its victims, its perpetrators, and its bystanders, we will explore the ways that the Holocaust has been memorialized, historicized, and fictionalized. Then, as a class, we will develop our own interpretative memorialization of this horrific moment in history.

description: This course familiarizes students with Cold War, twentieth-century Latin American history, including US imperialism and intervention in the region. We will ponder; what comes first (or has come first historically), counterrevolution or revolution? How much was anticommunist Cold War paranoia exactly that--a panicked witch hunt whose culprits did not exist or were exaggerated and demonized? How serious and successful were and are the revolutionary, leftist, and socialist politics of twentieth-century Latin America? We will explore why and how the US exported state terror, torture, and dictatorship to Latin America, as well as how homegrown local elite and common people made right-wing, anticommunist policies possible. The class will also document everyday Latin Americans such as campesinos (rural dwellers or peasants) turn to revolutionary and radical politics after being brutalized by counterinsurgency and policing.

description: This course introduces students to the study of physiological and functional adaptations to human movement. The field is richly interdisciplinary, involving such disciplines as anatomy, chemistry, biology, physics, physiology, biomechanics, motor control, psychology, nutrition, neuroscience, rehabilitative therapy, and exercise prescription. Rigorous and systematic study of these sub-fields enables students to understand how and why people move and the factors which limit and enhance the capacity to move. Offered annually.
name: Introduction to Kinesiology
notes: Open only to rising sophomores and incoming first-year students.

description: The course is rooted in advanced nutrition science and behavior-change psychology. Students examine the roles nutrient selection, metabolism, and timing play in supporting physical performance as well as mental and emotional health. Students discuss the integration and regulation of metabolism, energy expenditure, hydration, sleep, stress, and recovery; and they conduct an advanced overview of the functions of macronutrients, micronutrients, fluids, and supplements that are determinants of health and diseases. Offered annually. Prerequisite: BIO 143 and BIO 243; kinesiology major.
name: Nutrition and Metabolism
notes: Open only to rising seniors and rising juniors.
title: Performance Nutrition

description: This course will explore the different time periods in a woman's life starting at puberty, the time around pregnancy, perimenopause, and post menopause. Changes in hormones lead to potential challenges for sleep, nutrition, exercise, and general health. As women approach mid-life, the risk of chronic disease significantly increases potentially leading to a poorer quality of life. Prevention strategies relating to wellness, nutrition, and exercise will be discussed. Prerequisite: declared kinesiology major.

notes: This course is open only to senior, junior and sophomore Kinesiology majors.    ;All other majors by instructor consent.                                         ;Topics Title: Women's Health Across the Lifespan

description: This course is an interdisciplinary introduction to Latin America. A central theme is the complex and recurring dynamics of traditions and change that have characterized Latin America since its inception more than five centuries ago. This includes examining how traditions are constructed and change, how they are maintained and/or revitalized by mixing new with old, local with regional and global, ideology with practice, as well as how new traditions are formed. description: This course is a historical introduction to philosophy, a discipline which pursues fundamental questions about the nature of reality and our place within it. Students critically engage with philosophical works across multiple periods and perspectives, while developing their own point of view on major philosophical questions. Specific topics vary, but typical examples include: What can we know, and how can we know it? What is a meaningful life? Is reality objective? What is the self? Offered annually. Prerequisite: first-year student or sophomore standing.
name: Knowledge, Reality, and the Self
notes: Course has class-year limits and is open only to first-year and sophomore       ;students.

description: Literature provides rich resources for thinking through central philosophical questions, including the metaphysics and ethics of freedom; the problem of evil; the role of character in choice and action; the nature of morality; rebellion and human solidarity; God's existence and relation to the world; and the nature of truth. This course explores philosophical ideas in literary works of several different genres by studying plot, character, point-of-view, imagery, and symbolism. Offered periodically.
name: Philosophy in Literature
notes: Open only to incoming first-year students and rising sophomores.

description: This course is an introduction to PPE, an interdisciplinary field that pursues the powerful connections among its three defining disciplines (philosophy, politics, and economics). Students engage with core topics in the field - such as markets, collective action, justice, and public choice - from a variety of ideological perspectives, such as libertarianism, Marxism, liberalism, and feminism. They learn how to integrate different disciplinary approaches in application to both theoretical and policy debates. Not open to first-year students except by special permission. Offered annually during fall semester.
name: Intro to PPE (Phil, Politics, Econ)
notes: Not open to incoming first-year students.
title: Introduction to PPE

description: This course surveys the origins and development of ancient Greek philosophy from the Presocratics in the 6th century BCE through Plato and Aristotle in the 4th century BCE. Students read and analyze primary texts in translation in order to examine the historical foundations of philosophical issues in cosmogony, natural philosophy, metaphysics, epistemology, logic, psychology, and ethics. As time permits, the course may include writings from one or more of the Hellenistic schools of Epicureans, Stoics, and Skeptics. Offered annually. Prerequisite: one course in philosophy or permission of instructor.
name: Ancient Greek Philosophy
prerequisites: one course in philosophy or permission of instructor.

description: Formal systems of logic attempt to make principles of good reasoning explicit. This course introduces two such systems of logic: propositional and predicate calculus. Students learn to use formal techniques to analyze arguments and explore philosophical issues related to meta-theory, including consistency and completeness, the paradoxes of material implication, ontological commitment, and the interpretation of quantifiers. Offered annually.
name: Formal Logic

description: This course is a philosophical inquiry into the core commitments of Christian theism in the context of other world religions and naturalism. Central themes include beliefs about the existence and nature of God, the doctrines of the trinity and incarnation, redemption and ritual, human free will and responsibility, revelation and reason, religious experience, the problem of evil, different views of life after death, miracles and historical inquiry, and religious pluralism. Offered annually.
name: Philosophical Theology
notes: Open only to incoming first-year students and rising sophomores.

description: This course clarifies central concepts and distinctions developed in the literature of moral philosophy and applications of those concepts and distinctions to concrete moral problems that arise in the practice of medicine. Issues may include euthanasia, abortion, medical paternalism, allocation of scarce medical resources, culturally sensitive medical care, pandemics, and conflicts of loyalty in managed care. Readings are drawn from both philosophical and medical discussions. Offered annually.
name: Biomedical Ethics
notes: Not open to incoming first-year students.

description: This course examines the main Western ethical theories and their application to contemporary moral concerns. Theoretical issues may include rights, duties, virtue, hedonism, egoism, the relation between ethics and theology, the fact-value distinction, relativism, and pluralism. Students discuss current topics such as global economic justice, euthanasia, the death penalty, animal rights, censorship, racism, privacy rights versus public safety, reproductive ethics, and environmental ethics. Offered annually.
name: Ethics and the Good Life
notes: Not open to incoming first-year students.

Offered annually.

notes: Not open to incoming first-year students.

Students pay critical attention to how the Black intellectual tradition understands the meanings and moral implications of such ideas. Offered annually.

description: Pragmatism is a philosophical school of thought holding that the truth of our theories depends on their practical value. Students will explore the foundations of this deceptively radical view as it emerged in late 19th and early 20th Century America. And they will follow its more recent development through major innovations in metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, political philosophy, and the philosophy of science. Readings include William James, John Dewey, Richard Rorty, Elizabeth Anderson, and others. Prerequisite: two courses in philosophy, one of which must be either PHIL 235 or PHIL 236 or permission of the department chair.

By examining the range of health problems and diseases affecting diverse cultures, races, and ethnic groups, students gain understanding of epidemiology as the science of public health. Offered periodically to all St Olaf students in the fall semester. Prerequisites: PHS 150 preferred.

Working in interdisciplinary teams, students articulate questions and develop research and response proposals based on literature, data at hand and the skills acquired from prior courses including the OLE Core. Integrating viewpoints, assessment modalities and communication within the team and with external audiences are emphasized. Local and global issues are included. description: A basic introduction to astronomy, this course concentrates on how we know what we know. Students explore questions such as "How do we measure the distance to a star?" and "How do we know the universe is expanding?" In addition to studying the solar system, stars, black holes, galaxies, and the history of the universe, students engage in observation using the department's telescopes. Offered every other year. Does not count toward physics major. Prerequisite: proficiency in algebra and geometry.

title: Introductory Astronomy

description: This two-semester in-depth course addresses topics in classical and modern physics using algebra, geometry, and some calculus. The course is well suited for students of biology or chemistry or for those desiring a thorough introduction beyond the high school level. Physics 124 takes up the Newtonian mechanics of point particles (motion, mass, force, torque, energy, momentum, and gravitation), Einstein's reexamination of space time (relativity), and nuclear physics. Students attend lectures plus one 2.5-hour laboratory per week. Offered annually in the fall semester. Does not count toward physics major. Prerequisite: MATH 119 or MATH 120 or equivalent.

Students focus primarily on the relationship between the structure and physical properties of materials, on length scales ranging from millimeters to nanometers. Students research articles from the peer-review literature that highlight the latest developments in the field. Students also discuss the technological and societal impacts of different materials and their applications. Offered annually. Prerequisite: PHYS 244.

Topics include an examination of the conceptual framework of Quantum Mechanics, solution of the Schrodinger Equation for systems such as the harmonic oscillator and the hydrogen atom, and approximation methods for treating more complex systems and the interaction of radiation with matter. Students in this course are normally registered for PHYS 386 as well, in order to complete the requirements for the physics major. Offered annually in the fall semester. description: This course is an introduction to some of the central, interrelated concepts and questions of political theory. Some of the readings will be drawn from recognized classics in the field while others will arise from contemporary debates about political issues and cultural diversity within the U.S. The course pays considerable attention to historical shifts in political thought but is not designed to provide a chronology of the great Western political thinkers. Instead, this course aims to provoke and sustain a semester-long exploration of what it means to be a political actor -- that is, a citizen -- and what it means to think about politics. Offered annually.

description: In a democratic state, the media play an important role in linking the people to elected officials and political institutions. The course is principally concerned with this connection. By analyzing broad and varied forms of political communication and studying scholarship on the role of media in society, students explore the structure of American media with respect to political institutions, the effects media can have on individuals' political attitudes, and the role the media play in political campaigns and governance. Also counts toward media studies concentration. Prerequisite: none, but one course in political science is recommended.

description: The American presidency is one of the most powerful political offices in the world. The actions and policies of U.S. presidents influence domestic governance, global affairs, and democratic institutions. This course examines the presidency's powers, constraints, and responsibilities, exploring the political processes that shape it. We analyze contemporary developments and historical trends, addressing key questions about nominations, institutional evolution, personal leadership, and the impact of social and economic forces, with a focus on the 21st-century presidency. Offered annually during spring semester.
name: American Presidency
title: The American Presidency

Broadly centered around the question, "How do you know?," students focus on different methods of locating and collecting data, reviewing political texts and contested concepts, and constructing theoretical explanations of political phenomena. Offered each semester. Prerequisite: one previous course in department and a declared PSCI major. Non-majors may register with permission of instructor.

Students learn how scholarly research is evaluated, revised, and prepared for publication by reviewing manuscripts and participating in editorial workflows. The course also introduces the norms of scholarly publishing. Students may take this course a second time, serving as Senior Editors, with enhanced leadership roles and editorial opportunities. Offered annually during fall and spring semesters. Prerequisites: Junior or senior standing, PSCI 220 and 2 additional political science courses, or instructor permission. By introducing students to theories of modernization, dependency, world systems, order, class, revolution, state, and political economy, the course attempts to provide the framework for answering this question. Also counts toward Latin American studies major and Latin American studies and business and management studies concentrations.

description: Political parties have traditionally served to organize the American electoral process but not to govern. Is their role changing? This course examines party organization, candidate recruitment, campaign strategies, the role of the media, election financing, and citizen participation.

Also counts toward business and management studies concentration. Offered annually.

Also counts toward international relations concentration.

description: This research seminar examines foundational and contemporary questions in American politics through the lens of federalism and democratic governance. How does the federal structure shape political inequality, representation, and policy outcomes? What methodological approaches best illuminate the dynamics of American political institutions? Students will engage with both classic texts and cutting-edge empirical research, critically evaluating the methods scholars use to answer core questions about power, polarization, and democracy in the United States. The seminar emphasizes methodological literacy; students will assess how quantitative, qualitative, historical, and mixed-method approaches address central debates in the field. Through discussion leadership, peer review, and an original research project presented in conference format, students will develop skills essential for advanced study in political science. Prerequisites: PSCI 220 and one course in the subfield, or permission of instructor.

description: How do psychologists characterize the most basic aspects of the learning process? While some emphasis is on analysis of the behavioral viewpoint (Pavlov, Skinner), students also examine the ways current investigators apply these basic principles to problems in other fields. These include behavioral therapy for a variety of psychological disturbances, research on the neurobiology of drug reward, and analysis of consumer behavior. Students engage in hands-on activities as a part of the class to enhance their learning. Offered annually. Prerequisite: PSYCH 125.

description: This survey of cognition examines how we acquire (perception, attention, learning), store (memory), communicate (language) and use knowledge (thinking, judgment, problem solving, decision making, creativity). Such issues influence how we educate people, evaluate eyewitnesses in court, convince consumers to buy products, and improve our memory or attention. Students will engage in hands-on activities as a part of the class to enhance our study of the mind. Offered annually. Prerequisite: PSYCH 125.
name: Cognitive Psychology

description: After mastering the foundations of data science - especially data wrangling and visualization - in SDS 164, data science students are ready to explore impactful applications and deeper fundamentals. Programming fundamentals may include iteration, functions, conditions, data types, SQL, regular expressions, version control, and simulation - all in the context of real data. New applications may include text as data, geospatial mapping, networks, and web scraping to produce dynamic graphics - presented with attention to data ethics and reproducible research. Offered annually. Prerequisite: SDS 164: Data Science 1.

description: This course introduces students to the subject of machine learning. The primary focus is the development and application of powerful machine learning algorithms applied to complex, real-world data. Topics covered include linear regression, nearest neighbor models, k-means clustering, shrinkage methods, decision trees and forests, boosting, bagging, support vector machines, and hierarchical clustering. description: This course helps students explore the connections between society and their own lives. Students answer challenging questions such as "Do we have a 'human nature'?," "Why does social inequality exist?," "What is race?," and "How do societies change?" This course is open to first-year students or students in certain accredited programs. Open to all students when taught during the summer. Offered each semester.

description: How do anthropologists study other cultures? Peoples around the world create different realities through the ways they conceptualize experience (cultures) and how they organize themselves to do what they need to do (societies). Anthropologists describe and compare cultures and societies, focusing on different aspects such as family and kinship, inequality and power, religion and values, economy and technology, cultural and social change. This course is open to first-year students or students in certain accredited programs. Offered each semester.

description: Disasters and crises loom large. They are not singular events. Their effects spiral starting where the crises occur and spiraling outward globally. This course examines disasters worldwide and anthropological approaches to studying them. This involves learning about disasters through various media, documentary film, written ethnography, and critical social theory. Studying disasters reveals much about scientific and institutional attempts to manage and control them and how power is articulated in disaster (mis)management. Offered annually.
name: Disasters

description: This course explores the complex human interaction with drugs. The readings examine historical trajectories of substance use and the ways drugs shaped the development of societies. Students learn more about how drugs work biologically and socially, as well as reasons why drugs can create powerful forms of addiction that often resist treatment. Ethnographic evidence vividly depicts the layered intersection of drugs, addiction, and therapeutic intervention in the United States and elsewhere.
name: Drugs, Addiction, and Anthropology

description: Students explore the continuing significance of color, class, and immigration in the U.S., with a focus on the experiences and concerns of African Americans, Native Americans, Hispanics/Latinos, and Asian-Americans. The course examines the nature and functions of prejudice; the relationship among race, class and gender; the persistence of racism and inequality; and social policies and social movements intended to create greater social justice. Offered annually in the fall or spring semester.
name: Race/Class-Am Culture
notes: This course includes an academic civic engagement (ACE) component.
title: Race and Class in American Culture

description: How do people understand illness and healing? How does social inequality shape health? These are among the questions explored by medical anthropology. In this course students examine the ways people in different societies experience their bodies, by looking at AIDS in Haiti, old age in India, and childbirth in the United States. Students investigate diverse understandings of health, different means of promoting healing, and the role of power in providing medical care. Offered annually.
name: Medical Anthropology

description: Urban sociology investigates the complex interactions of human beings in cities and beyond. Topics include the changing relationship between people and place; social stratification along the lines of race/ethnicity, gender/sexuality, and class; and urbanism's importance in global political power and economics. Chicago will serve as an important case study for considering these social, political, and economic dynamics. Offered annually.
name: Urban Sociology

description: This core SOAN course covers critical concepts from Sociology and Anthropology to understand complex social and cultural dynamics systematically. Focusing on key concepts and thinkers that have shaped the disciplines of Sociology and Anthropology, the course will provide majors with the critical analytic tools important for subsequent courses that they will take.
name: Social Theory
notes: Open to SOAN Majors only

description: This anthropology course examines the ocean both as an object of study and as a tool by which to understand social, global, and cultural complexity. Today's economic and geopolitical imaginations are dictated by geographic territorialisms, primarily articulated by political forms such as nation states, area studies, and trenchant regionalisms. The course offers a "view from the boat" or an "oceanic perspective" to understand contemporary issues such as climate change, border crises, human-non-human relations, and resource extraction, while also expanding our understandings of history, global connection and exchange.
name: Top: AquaPolitics
notes: Full topic title: Aqua-Politics: Understanding the World Oceanically

description: Among English-speakers one sometimes hears references to "the power of love" and much is written about love, particularly the love between man and woman as well as family love (between parents and children, between siblings, between grandparents and grandchildren). At the same time some people deny human capacity to overcome difficulties and profound changes in life through love. Is it possible to sustain love between two people under extremely adverse conditions? Are there biological and social forces that 'drive us to love'? What matters at the end of a human life: the political, social, and economic history of a society or the history of the family? What has ultimate meaning: the history of a nation or the love of a committed couple based on shared perceptions, experiences, and esteem? Even among those who believe in the power of love, there are differing opinions with respect to the importance of the love of God. For many novelists toward the end of the past century and today, God does not appear to exist, or at least the force of God in human life is never communicated. In Spanish 314 we will explore these and other themes in a series of literary works written in Latin America. We will analyze not only the authors' perspectives but also the techniques employed to communicate them. Our particular focus will be the use of magical realism. Prerequisite: SPAN 275.

description: When we read a text that is distant from us, whether in time, space, cultural or social context, how do we overcome that distance? As writers, whether our aim is to create a text that pleases or persuades, how do we work towards closing the distance between ourselves and our readers? These are the general questions that we will wrestle with this semester. We will approach them head-on through readings and discussions of a world that will be so distant for many of us that we might not know anything about it at all -- medieval Eastern Europe. In so doing, we will find out how filthy vikings really were, how much bread a squirrel skin could buy in the tenth century, and finally what was an aurochs? By the end, we will gain a better understanding of how to approach texts produced by cultures and peoples that are profoundly distant from us and become better readers and writers in the process.

This seminar will begin with these literary utopias before considering historical attempts to make a "good place" in a real place and time. We'll investigate the common problems that both real and imagined utopias have tried to solve, and we’ll seek to understand the roots of these problems. Writing for the course will emphasize research, analysis, argumentation, and reflection.

description: This seminar is designed for students interested in language as action in "real life," literature, and performance. In each context, speakers seek to connect with and influence others through language. Questions we may address are: What makes a good conversation? Why (and when) do we lie? How does dialogue capture voices in personal narrative? What is a character trying to achieve through the words they speak in a scene? How does an actor convey and interpret intentions already present in the play's language? We'll seek to answer them through careful observation of our own conversations, readings in non-fiction and drama, and viewing live and filmed productions. Students synthesize these experiences and the results of their inquisitive research to write in several modes and genres. The writing process for these assignments integrates substantial time for workshops of drafts and students' reflections on their own rhetorical practices and development.

How has this obsession with placemaking (including our digital streets) impacted our conception of family, work, and community? How has the organization of our neighborhoods contributed to racism and socio-economic divides? Major assignments will include personal narratives and reflective journals, an op-ed, a creative project centering around town/city planning, and a major research essay.

description: How do we know what's ethical in a medical setting, and how can we explore those ethics through literature? Going a step further: how can reading and writing lead us to deeper insights about the nature of health itself, including the health of an individual, a group, or even a society? And how do processes of research and reflection inform the daily choices of readers, writers, and medical practitioners? As we explore a range of genres in this seminar, from illustrated memoir and drama to journalism and personal essays, we'll ask how literature and medicine can interact to teach us about observing details, setting priorities, and listening in ethical ways. By working on three sequenced portfolio collections of writing during the semester, each student will hone their own authorial voice before learning to engage with one other writer on a key medical debate, and finally host a research conversation between multiple cited sources.

description: Have you noticed that despite our unprecedented access to news, entertainment, and social networks, it can often seem harder to stay informed and easier to feel disconnected? This feeling has a history, and this course follows the rise of the modern media--from the transnational networks built in the 19th century to the growth of broadcast media in the 20th century and the rapid spread of social media in the 21st century. We not only explore the histories of technological change (the telegraph, the television, and the internet), but also grapple with the questions they have raised about knowledge, free speech, social fracture, and the future of democracy. Our daily experience of media is deeply personal, and through reading, conversation, and argumentative writing we will discover why our media landscape appears the way it does and how we can find a stable and healthy orientation within it.

description: Many people today yearn for slowness and connection with each other and the earth as we navigate ecological degradation, rising global autocracy, and accelerating AI automation. In this seminar, we trace the roots of these crises through reading and discussion, and work to imagine alternatives to our current society. Together, we explore what animals, plants, fungi, and water can teach us about liberation and living in right relations with our more-than-human world. We also practice a slow, salvage-and-repair writing process, composing messy first drafts without AI or automation, practicing research as a method to honor our intellectual "ancestors," and developing our voices as civic and public writers, imagining and contributing to livable futures for the common good.

description: Human beings have created and increasingly inhabit a digital world. Our reliance on computers, phones, and digital technology, however, is a recent development. How are our relationships with devices and technology altering us individually? Collectively? Evolutionarily? This seminar will examine the social, psychological, physical, and cultural impacts of computers, internet, smartphones, and AI. We will explore these impacts from different perspectives, including science, social science, and science fiction. Students will reflect on their technology habits, experiment with habit changes, and write a review, an argumentative essay, speculative fiction, and a research project on a topic of their choice.

description: What does it mean for art to be "good" or "bad?" For example, why does Instagram poetry raise questions about its validity as art? What about paintings that try to be ugly? What makes the film The Room "so bad it's good?" This seminar explores forms of "bad" and "ugly" art--specifically in poetry, visual art, and on the screen--that nevertheless attract attention and praise. Our reading, writing, and discussion aim to clarify the nature and the stakes of the most fundamental questions related to art, literature, and aesthetics. Does beauty have an essence that can be identified, qualified, and quantified independent of culture? Is there a connection between our sense of what is "beautiful" and our sense of what is "good" or "just" or "ethical"? We'll go beyond art to consider how our individual aesthetic tastes influence our friendships and relationship tastes. Students will read, view, watch, and write in order to learn about existing aesthetic theories and to develop their own. Major writing assignments will include a "letter of recommendation" for an object or text that you think is "beautiful" and a research project that examines an "ugly" work of art within the context of existing aesthetic theories.
name: Top: Art and Beauty
notes: Section topic: Art and Beauty: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly
title: Writing and Rhetoric

description: This seminar explores the use of writing as a way of engendering the body and its multiple identities: that is, the body as a sex, raced, queer, and non-normative matter. We will practice close reading through class discussions, personal essays, reflections, and short digital responses while engaging in a relational examination of how contemporary memoirs, essays, short fictions, and other narratives and media show the relationship between consciousness and the body. We will explore how writers narrate what it means to have a disabled, dying, diseased, or ethnically othered body, and how these different conditions are formally and thematically represented across genres and media. It centers how writers narrate embodied experiences, craft alternative spaces of kinship and belonging, love and acceptance, against limiting and normative social categories. To develop as writers, students will be expected to engage in close reading, to write critically and to develop their skills by engaging in regular peer review of each other’s writing (understanding writing as a process that improves through collaboration), and finally by composing a final paper or creative project on a course theme. Readings might include Marjane Satrapi, Lucy Grealy, Jamaica Kincaid, James Baldwin, Richard Rodríguez, and Gloria Anzaldúa. This seminar is ideal for students interested in feminism, queer thinking, and comparative race studies.
name: Top: Writing Self, Writing Body

description: How did we get from Richard Nixon and DJ Kool Herc's break to Obama's playlists and Cardi B? This writing course uses hip-hop culture as a guide to the social, political, economic, and artistic changes that have taken place in the US since the early 1970s. We will focus on the historical circumstances and unique spaces out of which hip-hop has arisen as well as the culture's own conceptions of history, social life, and aesthetics, or what you might call its poetics of place. Our study of hip-hop culture will encourage us to think about writing as a process, a practice of daily attention and development. To this end, you will learn to write in diverse formats, from close listening exercises and album reviews to personal reflection papers and a research-driven essay. As a class, we will participate in a semester-long series of workshops that will invite you to generate and circulate drafts among your peers, respond to and provide feedback on the work of others, and revise your writing.
name: Top: Hip-hop Cult/Poetics of Place
notes: Section topic: Hip-hop Culture and the Poetics of Place
title: Writing and Rhetoric

description: Environmental Humanities is the name given to the effort to bring together the humanities (literature, art, history, philosophy) and the sciences to address contemporary environmental problems like climate change. This approach recognizes the physical, cultural, and social elements that contribute to complex definitions of environment and environmental problems. In this seminar, we will explore a variety of texts that engage the sciences and humanities to appreciate the essential role that storytelling, poetry, cinema, and other creative genres play in bringing diverse voices and multicultural perspectives to understanding and addressing environmental issues. Students will write a narrative argument, critical analysis, and develop a research project based on a course theme or subject.
name: Top: Environmental Humanities
notes: Section topic: Environmental Humanities

description: Stephen Hawking once mused that "[c]omputers will overtake humans with AI within the next 100 years. When that happens, we need to make sure the computers have goals aligned with ours." Artificial Intelligence (AI) will fundamentally change our world; on this point, scientists, journalists, and creative writers all agree. How it will do so, and whether those changes are positive or catastrophic, is up for debate. In this seminar, we will delve into discussions about AI in the United States and Britain in the contemporary era (1850s-present) and analyze how we talk about AI: what it can do, what it can't (or shouldn’t) do, and what role humans should play in the process. This seminar does not require any technical knowledge and will not ask you to do any coding. Instead, we will read creative works, watch films, and play with generative AI platforms to look at representations of AI to understand how they shape our understanding of this technology, explore its impact on society, and consider its implications for our understanding of our own humanity.
name: Top: AI in Culture and Discourse
notes: Section topic: Artificial Intelligence / Analogue Ignorance?: AI in Culture and ;Discourse

description: Today and in the past, romantic love is a hotly contested theme in many kinds of narratives, including film, poetry, novels, plays, and cultural analyses. In this seminar, students write argumentative papers, interpretive essays, reflections, and other responses to love narratives from Shakespeare to early Hollywood film to contemporary memoir. The seminar will question why romantic love is such a widely celebrated subject, how it has changed over time, how its representation differs among cultures and subcultures, and how queer viewpoints, asexuality, and aromanticism have critiqued its assumptions. Class time will include discussion of assigned texts, workshopping of student writing, and in-class writing sessions.
name: Top: Romantic Love
notes: Section topic: Romantic Love
title: Writing and Rhetoric

description: What does it take to build a world from scratch - and what does the act of building one reveal about storytelling, culture, and imagination? Dungeons & Dragons has been inviting players to answer that question for over 50 years, drawing on a rich literary tradition that runs from Tolkien and Jack Vance to contemporary film, television, and live-play streams like Critical Role. In this seminar, we trace the literary DNA of D&D: the foundational texts that shaped the game, the world-building traditions they created, and how those traditions became a global cultural phenomenon. We treat world-building itself as a writing practice - a way of making arguments about how societies work, what we value, and what we fear. Major writing assignments will move from close analysis of texts and games to research-driven argumentation and reflection. Students will also learn practical skills for engaging AI as a thought partner to strengthen their own writing - learning how to use it and when not to use it. Students with reservations about AI will always have non-AI alternatives. No prior experience with D&D is required or expected.
name: Top: Dungeons & Dragons
notes: Section topic: Dungeons & Dragons and the Literary Imagination

description: What if we understand clarity in writing to mean not just the difference between usable and inaccessible, but also between just and violent? In this course, we will explore how clarity, or a lack thereof, shapes our experience with interpersonal and institutional power. We'll begin with the Plain Writing Act signed by President Obama in 2010, which requires federal agencies to make their documents clearer and more usable. This legislation argues that clarity will make government language more accessible to the public and by extension, yet perhaps more importantly, that it will reduce federal spending on paperwork. To explore how people communicate with diverse audiences when justice is at stake, we will analyze texts ranging from workplace emails to college marketing copy to legal prose and even long-term nuclear waste warning systems. Students in this class will develop practical rhetorical skills, including the Plain Language style guide, while also considering broader questions about language, power, and responsibility.
name: Top: Plain Language is Justice
